## Version 1.1

<p class="note">12 October 2026, 282 changes</p>

<h3>The few that matter most</h3>

<ul>
<li><b>Export data</b>: the bench’s readouts, plots, screens’ rays and fields, beams, sweeps and parts as CSV or JSON (a free account), or Excel, NumPy and MATLAB files (JEKrayPro); <code>save()</code> in Scripts.</li>
<li><b>Exports with a free account</b>: pictures, plots, data, .zmx and CAD files; a .jekray file needs none. <b>Free account</b> and <b>Pro</b> badges mark what needs what.</li>
<li>A <b>3D view</b> of every bench, a switch away: every free-space part placed, tipped and rolled in all six degrees of freedom, with rays, Gaussian beams and the diffracted field followed exactly through it, misaligned cavities included.</li>
<li><b>STL objects</b> from CAD on the bench (mounts, housings, baffles), saved with it and kept in My parts.</li>
<li><b>Electronics</b> as a standard part of the tool, with <b>feedthroughs</b> carrying signals between tabs, and photonic chips wired to them.</li>
<li><b>JEKrayPro</b> in open beta: benches in the cloud with their history, My benches and My parts, and the designers’ design work (the optimiser, tolerancing, reports, drawings and export); and the <b>documentation</b>, with the equations behind every model.</li>
<li><b>Draw</b> on the bench for figures, and export just the view you have framed.</li>
<li>Smoother all round: sweeps that render the field play every step, parts drag smoothly in 3D, and long sums run in the background.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Every change</h3>

<ul>
<li>Changing a sweep’s <b>Steps</b> (or pressing Play) on a bench that is slow to trace no longer holds the page while every step is traced first: on one bench that was 48 seconds for 30 steps, and read as a crash. The steps are seen to in the background, and a field shared by every step is worked out once, not once a step.</li>
<li>A sweep that leaves the beams as they are (a particle turned, a part moved off the beam) now works out every step: it was judged too large for memory by its one shared field and rendered one step in three, the rest showing a stale picture of the particle’s light. Ticking a particle’s <b>Draw an estimate of its scattered field</b> or <b>Draw its radiation pattern in 3D</b> off while a sweep plays no longer traces every step again. A paused sweep keeps what was worked out, and its slider goes to the sweep’s own steps, so pulling it shows each at once. A rod tilted by half a turn more is the same rod, so its scattering is solved once for both: a sweep right round solves half as many.</li>
<li>The <b>electrical feedthrough</b> has one connector, as a node has: a signal wired into it goes on from it on the same tab and from its partner on the other. It had an in and an out, and its out gave only what went into its partner, so a generator into a feedthrough and on to a scope on one tab read nothing. Benches saved with the old two connectors open as they were.</li>
<li>A photodiode’s oscilloscope in <b>Roll</b> follows a sweep: while any sweep plays it plots the reading against the sweeps’ own time, a point a step over the last cycle, the level and each beat’s swing as lines of their own (it stood still before, three beat periods wide). <b>Draw light by its power</b> is now <b>Fade weak rays and beams</b>, under Show the rays. <b>View › True colour field in 3D</b> draws the diffracted field in the light’s own colours, so white light through a prism fans out from red to blue. In 3D the wheel zooms towards the point the view is being turned about while the turn is held, and for a moment after. <b>How the rays look…</b> is with the experimental features for now.</li>
<li>Sweeps, steadier: a sweep’s <b>Steps</b>, <b>From</b> and <b>To</b> are taken when you press Enter or leave the box, not at each digit (every digit used to start its render again). A sine or triangle sweep works each position out once, not once on the way up and again on the way down, so its field renders in about half the time. After a change of Steps a field too large for memory keeps to the steps that fit. A rod’s <b>Axis tilt up</b> swept past 180° comes round (0 to 360° turns it right round). Ticking a screen’s <b>Show the diffraction pattern on its face</b> while a sweep plays no longer makes it stutter, and turning 3D on while the field is still arriving no longer leaves every later field to be worked out on the page.</li>
<li>A sweep with Steps blank no longer takes a new value at every frame: it plays on an automatic fixed set of steps, about 30 a second at its rate (from 48 up to 600 a cycle, shown in the Steps box as <i>auto</i>), the same points its field is rendered at. Each cycle comes back to the same values, so every step is traced, lit and its Particle solved once and then reused, its scattered light added all at once like the field, and the rays always match the field. Steps typed in now go up to 600.</li>
<li>A sweep follows the bench: the <b>Render the diffracted field</b> tick is gone. With the diffracted field shown (Light), Play starts the sweep at once with the parts, rays, beams’ outlines and readings, works the field out for its steps in the background under its bar, and adds it to every step at once when it is ready; a Particle’s scattered light comes the same way, each when it is ready, so no step shows a layer another lacks. With the field off, none is worked out. The 30-second hold, the bench frozen while a long render went on, is gone where the sweep can play beside it. A bench saved with the tick opens with its own Light setting deciding.</li>
<li>A bench opens in <b>2D</b> again; the 2D / 3D switch at the bench’s bottom right turns 3D on, and a tab keeps the view chosen for the visit.</li>
<li>Turning the 3D view while a sweep plays its rendered field no longer stutters at each step. A sweep that comes back to a value (a triangle sweep of a rod’s tilt, on its way up and down) had its light, the particle’s scattered glow among it, built again at every step of every cycle; now each step’s light is built once and then shown as it is. A cavity on the bench with no light to settle in is no longer solved again at every step, and the scattered light past the parts is built faster.</li>
<li>A <b>Particle</b> can draw its radiation pattern in 3D: tick <b>Draw its radiation pattern in 3D</b> under On the bench on its Scattering tab. A see-through surface about the particle reaches out in each direction as far as it scatters that way, on a linear scale whatever the Scale, so a small sphere’s doughnut and a rod’s lobes can be seen, turning with the particle and following a sweep. Off unless asked for.</li>
<li>A sweep held while its steps are worked out no longer leaves the bench stretched or blank when a panel opens or closes beside it, in 2D or 3D.</li>
<li>A <b>Particle</b> made a rod or a spheroid with Model set to Mie now uses the dipole array, so its scattering follows its shape and how it is turned (Mie holds for a sphere only); the Scattering tab says so.</li>
<li>The page stays free while the light catches up. A sweep that renders its field on a bench slow to trace (fibres, a Particle, many parts) takes each step’s trace from the worker that rendered it or solved its particle, so its first cycle plays without tracing every step on the page (on a bench with fibres and a Particle, a wait of a fifth of a second at each step); a Particle’s answer comes with the bench traced with it, so the page does not trace it again as the answer arrives. Every such trace is checked against a fresh one on the examples. A receiving horn’s coupling is worked out faster, to the same numbers. The 3D view works out the field’s glow at half the size each way while it turns, pans or zooms and while a sweep plays, and at full size again once it is still. A sweep whose rendered field would not fit in memory (the levitated-trap example: 240 steps of 140 MB) renders every so many steps rather than closing the tab.</li>
<li>Sweeps play closer to real time. Each step’s trace is kept while a sweep plays, on benches with fibres, circuits and particles as well, so the next cycle, and a sweep played over its steps rendered ahead, draws them without tracing again. A kept trace is used only where it is exactly a fresh trace’s (checked on every example). A sweep that asks for more steps a second than the computer can draw skips steps to keep its time, and its panel says so. The rays are drawn at the screen’s resolution while it plays. A levitated-trap bench with its particle’s field drawn plays its pre-rendered 48-step polarisation sweep at about 35 frames a second in 2D, where it managed 8.</li>
<li>A sweep whose work ahead (its diffracted field, a Particle’s scattering) is predicted to take longer than 30 seconds no longer plays its steps as they trickle in: the bench stays as it is and the progress bars say how long is left (“about 1 min 20 s left”), then the whole cycle plays smoothly. The prediction is made again as each step finishes, and Pause still stops it at once. Every progress bar now has a light running along it while its work goes on, so a slow one is plainly still working (with reduced motion, it breathes gently instead).</li>
<li>A <b>Particle</b>’s Dipoles across reads 0 as automatic, and says under it what automatic picks.</li>
<li>A <b>Particle</b> is far quicker to sweep and to edit. Its scattering is linear in its light, so once two polarisations are solved every other polarisation and power is their combination, checked on the field and never assumed: a 20-step sweep of a fibre laser’s polarisation on a 1 µm sphere went from about 100 s a cycle to 3 s, and as a dipole array from 108 s to 4 s. Every answer is kept, so a sweep’s next cycle, and a value typed back, show at once. A sweep solves the particle’s steps ahead, beside the field, with a bar of its own under the bench’s (“Scattering … step 7 of 20”) and in the Scattering tab, and each frame shows its own step. The dipole array sums its dipoles by FFT and starts each solve from the nearest answer (a 4000-dipole rod: 10 s a step to 1 s), the trap is found only when the Trap tab is read, a solve made out of date is stopped rather than left to run, and a rod’s <b>Axis tilt</b> goes past 90° to 180°, so a tilt sweep can carry it through upright. Numbers typed in a panel reach the bench once typing pauses, so a key never waits on a slow bench.</li>
<li>Fibres no longer swing out in great loops in 3D when a bench opens straight there: their routes in 3D no longer depend on how the 2D bench is zoomed.</li>
<li>Right-click a part and choose <b>Suppress</b> to take it out of the bench until it is wanted again, as CAD suppresses a feature: it is not drawn, in 2D or 3D, a click does not pick it, and nothing meets it: the light passes where it stood, and the fibres and wires plugged into it count as unplugged at its end. Several selected suppress together. The Bench panel’s list keeps it, struck through: right-click it for <b>Unsuppress</b>. Undo, the file and share links keep it; in a script, <code>J.suppress(name, on)</code>.</li>
<li>A <b>Particle</b> can draw an estimate of its scattered field, as the diffracted field is drawn, on the bench and in 3D: tick <b>Draw an estimate of its scattered field</b> on its Scattering tab. It is the far-field pattern falling off as 1/r², stopped at the first part each direction meets, the intensity alone, on a log scale of its own (the scattered light is a millionth of the beam or less), so the beam is drawn as it was. It has cool colours of its own (navy to cyan on the dark bench), told apart from the beam where they overlap; the 3D key gives its scale under the beam’s, and pointing at it reads it; and while it is drawn the particle’s fan and cone rays are faded to 30% so they do not clutter it. Past a lens, or any part that passes it on, it goes on as a glow drawn from the cone’s rays (each ray’s power over the tube it and its neighbours bound), joining the picture where the light enters the part and on the same scale. It follows the Scattering tab’s <b>Scale</b>, which the figure takes too: Linear, or Logarithmic over 30, 40 (the default), 60 or 90 dB (in 3D, along a line of sight, half the dB); a deeper scale draws it further out. Off unless asked for. The switches for a particle’s light on the bench (sending it to the parts, the fan, this picture) are together on its Scattering tab, under <b>On the bench</b>.</li>
<li>A part hidden by its eye in the bench list is hidden on the 2D bench as well as in 3D, its name with it, and a click there no longer picks it; the light still meets it, and chosen in the list it is drawn faintly. A <b>Particle</b>’s sign shrinks with the bench when zoomed out (never larger than 1 mm there), so it no longer dwarfs the parts round it.</li>
<li>A <b>Particle</b> inside a two-mirror cavity is solved in the cavity’s own Hermite-Gauss modes: its light that goes round and comes back drives it again, every round trip at once, by Mie, the dipole array or the single dipole. The Scattering tab gives how far it moves the cavity’s resonance and how much it widens it, and the detectors behind either mirror read the cavity with the particle in it. A ring, or a cavity clipped or out of line, keeps the warning.</li>
<li>A <b>Particle</b> in a concentric or confocal cavity, or one near them, is solved too: the mirrors bring its light back re-imaged, so it is solved over the directions it sends onto them, each traced round the cavity by the bench’s tracer (the mirrors’ shape, rims, coatings and placing), every return of it followed until it fades. The detectors read the cavity with the particle in it. A cavity of small Fresnel number gets a note that the rims are taken as hard edges.</li>
<li>A <b>Particle</b> in a retro-reflected beam is driven by its own scattered light coming back as well, scattered again until it settles (second scattering), whether it is a sphere, a rod or spheroid (the dipole array is solved again each pass) or a single dipole: the scattered power moves by up to 2.5% in the validation case, and its energy balances. Inside a cavity, where the light would come back again and again, the Scattering tab says it is not modelled.</li>
<li>A <b>Gaussian beam</b> through a curved face now passes what its whole footprint passes, each part at its own angle, in place of what its axis ray passes: behind a steep bare lens it reads lower (2.4% in the optical tweezers example). A steep focus takes a round beam’s field by its series (8e-4 on an NA 0.8 focus). The Trap tab gives no depth or frequencies where nothing is held.</li>
<li>A <b>Particle</b> is lit by beams that rise or descend out of the bench plane (after a tipped laser, a tipped mirror or a periscope), each taken in its own frame; its scattered light reaches the parts beyond as it does from a level beam. A screen’s atom trap in a rising beam is now where the beam meets the screen (it was looked for further along).</li>
<li><b>A particle is a Particle part</b>: a screen’s Trap tab is for atoms, and screens no longer have a Scattering tab. A bench saved with a particle on a screen opens with it moved onto a Particle part of its own, with every setting it had, where the screen’s beam met it, and its Trap and Scattering figures are as they were. As a Particle it also sends its scattered light onto the bench.</li>
<li>A <b>Particle</b>’s scattered light: two cones that reach one detector now add as fields when the same laser drives them (a particle seen directly and in a mirror, two particles in one beam), as each already did with the unscattered beam; cones driven by different lasers add as powers. A bench with a Particle retraces about twice as fast: a ray’s tube area on a detector comes from its neighbours in the cone, in place of two extra rays each, and the parts with a clear line to the particle are only looked for again when a part or the particle moves. The validation page has a new case, a split detector’s signal for a sphere in an NA 0.8 focus against an independent calculation, and others: a sphere at the focus of a real glass asphere against an independent trace of the same lens, and a sphere in a retro-reflected focus, its standing wave and both detectors, tight and gentle. Scattered light that has passed through a focus on its way now takes that focus’s Gouy phase, so the light a mirror brings back through the particle’s focus adds to the light scattered straight back as it should; a gentle beam that comes back on itself is read against the beams where they land, and a cone meeting a beam at a steep angle on a detector no longer adds fringes the rays cannot see.</li>
<li><b>A part’s own colours</b>: every part’s panel has a <b>Colours</b> section with a <b>Line colour</b> and a <b>Fill colour</b> (and Default, to go back). The part is drawn in them on the bench and in every export; its glass stays as see-through as it was. Several parts selected together take a colour at once. <b>Export figure</b>, Journal and Technical drawing, has <b>Parts</b>: In their colours, or <b>Black and white</b> (black lines, white fills, the light still in its colour unless Light is Black too, the light inside a fibre with it). A fibre or a wire has a <b>Line colour</b> of its own too: click it, and it is in its panel.</li>
<li><b>Fibre tips and collimators are single-mode</b>, as the fibres and fibre parts they join are: the Multimode choice is gone from a tip’s panel. A tip saved as multimode opens as the standard single-mode fibre (4.4 µm core, NA 0.12), so the light it takes in is now its mode’s overlap, and less than it read before.</li>
<li><b>Export figure</b>: a name you placed by hand keeps its place unless it stands where another part’s name has to go; then it is set with the rest, if that leaves fewer names led out on lines.</li>
<li><b>Export figure</b>: ports are small dots; a fibre part’s value (1550 nm, 25 dB, 1 GHz) is given with its name, not as a small tag that the figure’s scale could put under something; <b>Light</b> can be <b>Left out</b>; a beam that leaves the bench with nothing to meet is drawn a short way and stops; a name that has to be led out goes where its line is shortest and crosses least.</li>
<li>A fibre tip’s own fibre is drawn as far as its port: zoomed out, and on an exported figure, there was a gap between the tip and the fibre joined to it.</li>
<li><b>Particle</b>, a new part (Add, Active and atomic): one small sphere, rod or spheroid placed anywhere on the bench, in whatever light reaches it. The light passes it untouched, and what it scatters goes on to the parts that can see it. Each such part is sent a cone of rays carrying the scattered field: its power in that solid angle, its polarisation and its phase, as light of the laser that drives the particle. A collection lens collimates it, a photodetector reads it and adds it to the unscattered beam as a field, a fibre tip takes its overlap with its mode. The particle’s <b>Scattering</b> tab lists the share of the scattered power each part catches and what none does; its <b>Trap</b> tab reads the trap the light makes for it. A faint fan shows the pattern in every direction, in 2D and over the whole sphere in 3D, and the Particle tab switches it off. A photodetector can be <b>Split in four</b>, to read right less left and top less bottom: behind a collection lens that is the position signal of a particle in a focus. A screen can still hold a particle, as before. The example <i>Light scattered by a 300 nm sphere</i> now has the particle, two collection lenses and two detectors. In scripts, <code>scattered(name)</code> gives the shares.</li>
<li><b>A part’s own colours</b>: every part’s panel has a <b>Colours</b> section with a <b>Line colour</b> and a <b>Fill colour</b> (and Default, to go back). The part is drawn in them on the bench and in every export; its glass stays as see-through as it was. Several parts selected together take a colour at once. <b>Export figure</b>, Journal and Technical drawing, has <b>Parts</b>: In their colours, or <b>Black and white</b> (black lines, white fills, the light still in its colour unless Light is Black too).</li>
<li><b>Export figure</b>, Journal and Technical drawing: the names are all one size (a name scaled on the bench no longer carries its scale into the figure), each is set clear of the parts and of the other names, with a thin line to its part when it has to go further out, a name at the edge is no longer cut, and the ports’ names are left out unless <b>Port names</b> is set to Shown. A bench too crowded for names is numbered, with a key under the figure (<b>Names</b>).</li>
<li>Faster on benches with a multimode fibre and a broad spectrum (an amplifier’s spontaneous emission, a modulator’s sidebands): the light coupled back into a multimode tip is worked out once for each beam that has not moved, and many times faster when it has; in 3D, beams that run the same path at the same size are drawn as one envelope. A fibre EOM no longer puts sidebands on an amplifier’s spontaneous emission (a slice of it is far wider than the drive frequency, so they changed nothing but the number of beams to follow). A bench that took 13 s to open and 8 to 12 s to answer a moved part now takes under 2 s and about a third of a second, with the same readings.</li>
<li><b>Scattering by a particle</b>: a screen’s new <b>Scattering</b> tab gives the light one small particle scatters. A sphere is worked out exactly (Lorenz–Mie); a rod with flat or round ends or a spheroid, at any orientation, as an array of dipoles (the discrete dipole approximation, run in the background with a Stop); and a single dipole (Rayleigh) is kept beside them to compare. The light is what the bench puts on the particle: a tight focus as its full vector field, every sample of its pupil a plane wave onto the particle, so the particle may sit off the focus; a gentler beam as a plane wave; beams of one laser added as fields. It reads the scattering, extinction and absorption cross-sections, efficiencies and asymmetry, the power scattered, the forward and back shares and the share a lens of a given NA would collect, with polar plots in the bench plane and out of it and a map over every direction. The particle is the Trap tab’s, now with a shape, gold, silver and aluminium among its materials, and water as a medium. In 3D the particle is drawn in its shape and orientation, enlarged so it shows. In a script, <code>JEKray.scatter(name)</code> and <code>JEKray.mie(x, mr, mi, angles)</code>. A new example, <b>Light scattered by a 300 nm sphere</b>, and two cases on the validation page.</li>
<li>The diffracted field behind a <b>hard edge</b> (a slit, a comb of slits, a knife edge, an iris or a rim off the beam’s axis) has its true amplitude. Each sample at an edge took its share of open area and the whole field was then scaled up to the open area’s power: the peak behind slits a few samples wide read up to 12% high, the envelope of an N-slit pattern came out narrow, and the fringes behind a straight edge lost contrast away from it. An edge is now carried as the samples can hold it exactly, with the light it sends past the grid’s reach kept at the top of that reach, so the power is still the open area’s. Slits that run the whole way up no longer cut the beam’s wings off above and below them (2% of a focus behind them). Behind an edge the field is sampled more finely where the grid can still hold the light. New on <a href="/jek/tools/jekray-validation.html#fresnel-edge">the validation page</a>: Fresnel’s fringes at a straight edge and the pattern of 2, 5 and 10 slits.</li>
<li>A <b>phase mask finer than the beam</b> (a phase grating, a diffuser, an SLM’s pattern) keeps its light. Behind a mask that spreads the light without cutting it, the diffracted field’s grid now grows with the light as it does behind an edge; before, a grating’s orders ran off the grid’s sides and were lost with no warning. The beam goes on along the mask’s mean slope across its footprint, where it took the slope under its own ray (a sinusoidal grating sent it off at βλ/d, a fork hologram’s core ended it once rays left the bench plane), and takes its focus from the trend of the slope across it. A sinusoidal phase grating’s orders now carry Jₙ(β)² each, on <a href="/jek/tools/jekray-validation.html#phase-grating">the validation page</a>. Light a mask sends past what the grid can carry is flagged.</li>
<li>A beam of M² above 1 keeps all its modes past its first surfaces: they shared one budget of 60 segments in the 2D field, so a beam of M² = 4 (36 modes) lost its weakest, widest ones after a lens and read 4% narrow. Each mode now has the budget of its own, as the estimate of the run’s time already took it.</li>
<li><b>The design work needs only a free account now</b>: the optimiser, tolerancing, design reports, lens drawings, design export, scripts, and data as Excel, NumPy or MATLAB files, any number of kinds at once. JEKrayPro is the cloud: benches saved online with their history, forks, My parts, teams, and more than a free account’s three share links.</li>
<li><b>Saving a bench as a .jekray file needs a free account</b> (Save, Ctrl+S). Signed in or not, the bench is kept in this browser as you work, with its earlier versions and Open recent.</li>
<li>The examples send their rays in <b>hexapolar rings</b> (3, 5 or 7 across: 7, 19 or 37 rays), so in 3D each beam fills its round aperture: the lenses, mirrors and traps, the interferometers, the RF horns and the fibre launches. A source of one guide ray, a slit, a pulse and the double slit keep a line.</li>
<li>The Bench panel’s list of parts reads as JEKcad’s feature list: one line a part, its kind small beside it, under a heading for each kind (free space, fibre, circuits, objects, drawings) with its count; the parts selected are marked, and the eye shows on hover (or while the part is hidden in 3D).</li>
<li>In 3D the bar no longer shows the Parts / Draw switcher: Parts is the only mode there (Draw is for the 2D bench).</li>
<li><b>Mates, and parts moved together, in 3D</b>: <b>Mate</b> on the 3D view’s bar holds two parts together. Click a face of the part that stays (a flat face, a round one such as a hole, a shaft or a lens’s rim, or close to a straight edge), then one of the part to move, and choose how they meet: <b>Coincident</b> (flush, facing each other), <b>Concentric</b> (on one axis), <b>Parallel</b>, a <b>Distance</b> apart or at an <b>Angle</b>, with Flip. The second part, with its group, moves to meet the first, and from then on the two move and turn together until the mate is deleted; each part’s panel lists its mates, to change a distance, an angle or Flip, or delete one. Undo takes any of it back, and mates are saved with the bench. In 3D, <b>drag across empty space</b> to select a boxful (Shift-click adds a part); the arrows and rings of several selected move them as one and turn them about their middle, and their panel moves and turns them by numbers typed. <b>Group</b> and <b>Ungroup</b> are on the bar too.</li>
<li>The 3D view’s <b>Model</b> tools (sketches extruded and revolved) are gone: objects come onto the bench by importing them (.stl, .step), and a CAD app of our own is in development. A part modelled with them before opens as the fixed object it made, where it was.</li>
<li><b>Coatings are designed in JEKfilm</b>, the new coating designer, in its own tab. A face’s <b>Design a coating in JEKfilm…</b> (and Tools › Coating design in JEKfilm…) opens it on that face’s glass and stack; saved to the cloud in the bench’s folder, the coating comes back onto the face. An RF lens’s matching layer is still designed here. Coatings you kept by name are still in every face’s Coating list, and JEKfilm can open them.</li>
<li><b>JEKfilm coatings on a face.</b> A face’s Coating list offers the JEKfilm coatings (◆) kept in the cloud bench’s folder, and a .jekfilm file from your computer. The face keeps a copy of the stack, linked to the coating: when the coating is saved again in JEKfilm, the bench offers to update its faces.</li>
<li>Fixed: a vapour cell in a magnetic field puts the ground state’s levels where they are measured to be. It took the electron’s own g-factor for the ground state; the measured g<sub>J</sub> (Steck’s, Tiecke’s) is larger by 1 part in 10<sup>5</sup> for rubidium and 1 in 10<sup>4</sup> for caesium, which moved caesium’s levels by 0.15 MHz at 1000 G. The validation page compares them with the Breit–Rabi formula.</li>
<li><b>Make the part</b>, under a lens’s drawing in the Optical designer: set what the lens or window is made to (quantity, diameter and thickness tolerances, centring, and face by face its finish, surface form, scratch-dig and chamfer; each one not set follows the tolerance settings or a commercial grade), and download its drawing, its part specification and each JEKfilm coating’s specification as one zip, ready to send to an optics maker. The element data’s Coating list offers JEKfilm coatings (◆) and a .jekfilm file, and the face keeps what the coating was designed to.</li>
<li>Fixed: a sweep that renders the diffracted field keeps every frame it rendered through what does not change the light: pausing and playing again, moving a part the light never reaches (or a drawing), changing <b>Field intensity</b> (linear or logarithmic is how the field is drawn, so it is drawn again at once) and the Light ticks. An edit that does change the light renders the field again for the bench as it now is and plays on. In 3D every step of the sweep is kept (a sweep of 120 steps lost its first ones each cycle), and its steps share one brightness scale, so light before an absorber whose density is swept stays as bright while the light after it dims.</li>
<li>Fixed: turning the 3D view while a sweep plays stayed choppy with an oscilloscope showing in Roll (each step solved its circuit again, tracing the bench for every photodiode, at ten frames a second): a beam that lands well inside a round part is no longer summed point by point, an amplifier’s clipping check is worked out once and from a table, and while sweeps play the scope solves afresh only as often as it can without taking the view’s frames.</li>
<li>Fixed: in 3D, turning the view while a sweep plays is smooth: the view is drawn once a frame however fast the pointer moves, and a sweep’s step that leaves the light and the cables where they were keeps their models and shadows rather than making them again.</li>
<li>Fixed: changing a sweep’s Steps while it renders or plays its diffracted field renders it again at the new steps and plays on (it was left working the field out live at every step, never catching up).</li>
<li>Fixed: a beam wider than a part it passes, the part above or below it or tipped, lost the light that missed the part. A gain sheet now amplifies only the light inside its disc; the rest goes on past it unchanged, in the beams, the field and the 3D view, and a detector after it reads both.</li>
<li><b>JEKsuite</b> has its mark at the bar’s far left, as in JEKion: it opens every bench of every app in its own tab (the same tab each time), signed in or not. It takes the place of the cloud button.</li>
<li>Fixed: in 3D, a sweep that renders the diffracted field now plays through its steps as fast as they can be drawn (each step waited four seconds, for the 2D field, which is not drawn in 3D); and the 3D field could stay at “working out” until the page was reloaded after a part was dragged into a beam (a request left waiting on a stopped worker).</li>
<li>Fixed in the optimisers: Undo after <b>Let the optimiser find it</b> in an exercise puts the start back (it went back past the exercise); the bench optimiser gives the same answer each time it is run on the same bench, and a peak narrower than its first scan’s step is no longer lost; the Optical designer’s global search brings a design that breaks the limits set on its values within them, as the local optimiser does; the coating designer never hands back a stack worse than it was given, and a blank thickness starts at a quarter wave.</li>
<li><b>JEKsuite</b>, the JEK hub: My benches is now a page of its own, <a href="/jek/tools/jeksuite.html" target="_blank">JEKsuite</a>, in its own tab, with every bench you keep in the cloud from every JEK app, JEKray’s and JEKion’s, labelled and filtered by app. Open either app from it, start a bench in one (or straight into the Optical, RF or coating designer), and manage your account, plan, billing and teams there. A bench chosen there opens here (the bar’s cloud button and File › My benches on JEKsuite take you to it).</li>
<li><b>Light drawn by its power</b>, on for every bench: each ray and each beam’s envelope, in 2D and 3D, is as bright as the power it carries against the brightest source on the bench, on a log scale over four decades (a sixteenth plainly there, a five-thousandth all but gone, below a ten-thousandth not drawn). Light fades as a splitter, a filter or a polariser takes it, and a crystal’s second harmonic brightens and dims as it comes into and out of phase matching. Untick <b>Draw light by its power</b> under Light to draw every beam at full strength; scripts read and set it as <code>J.project().light.byPower</code>.</li>
<li>A sweep that renders the diffracted field takes enough frames to play smoothly at its rate (about 30 a second, up to 240 a cycle), so a slow sweep glides rather than steps; Steps still sets its own number.</li>
<li>The bench JEKray opens with now has a Gaussian beam as well as its rays, so its envelope and diffracted field show (it was rays alone).</li>
<li><b>Fibres in 3D</b>: click a fibre, wire or waveguide in the 3D view to select it (its panel opens), and drag it across the table to shape it, as on the bench. A fibre now leaves each connector straight and level, its face square to the ferrule. The bench’s <b>notes</b> moved to Edit › Bench notes…, and <b>My benches</b> is the cloud beside the bench’s name, apart from Examples.</li>
<li><b>The Bench panel comes out on the left</b>, from the tab on the bench’s left edge, so it is plain which panel is the bench’s, and it stays out while you select parts; a part’s panel opens on the right, and closes with its ×. Opening or closing either no longer shifts the bench: what is drawn stays where it was. Fixed: <b>Show the rays</b> ticked on a bench saved with them off now shows them. <b>How the rays look</b> (brightness by power, fading trails, glow, width) has a window of its own, View › How the rays look…. The longer explanations left the panels for the Help menu: <b>Using the bench</b> and <b>About the selected part</b>.</li>
<li><b>From Instagram</b>: every link from our Instagram posts now opens the Michelson interferometer example with its moving mirror sweeping, and the note listing our reels’ benches has gone. The bench JEKray opens with sends its rays in hexapolar rings, a full beam in 3D.</li>
<li><b>Getting JEKrayPro is simpler</b>: a <b>Get Pro</b> button in the bar, and every Pro feature, open the plans and prices, signed in or not. Pay straight away: your account is made from the address you pay with, and you are signed in when you come back. The <b>academic price</b> needs only your university email address, typed beside it (no code to wait for); any of the 10,000 universities in a public register counts. Menu items that need an account or JEKrayPro are no longer greyed: their badge says what they need. Signing in by email sends a link you click (the code still works), and you stay signed in for a year. Checking for a university licence now says plainly when yours has none.</li>
<li><b>No ticks for a source’s light</b>: a source always traces its rays, and a new one propagates a Gaussian beam; its panel’s <b>Field</b> says what its field starts from, the Gaussian beam or even illumination across the fan (a uniform pupil, for a lens’s Airy pattern, Strehl and MTF). A fibre tip always sends both. The bench’s <b>Light</b> turns the rays, or the beams, off for every source at once. The look of the rays (brightness by power, trails, glow, width) is folded under its own heading. JEKray opens in the <b>Dark</b> theme (View › Theme) and in <b>3D</b> (2D at the bottom right), with the Bench panel showing and a thinner bar, and a share link opens straight into its bench.</li>
<li>A scope’s <b>Offset</b> works with its scale on auto: typing one keeps the scale on the screen as Per division (wide enough to keep the trace in view), so the trace moves as on a bench scope; before, it was ignored until Per division was set. In 3D, a fibre component or circuit part dragged across the table now moves with its fibres (and Ctrl+Z puts it back), its arrows from the middle of its body.</li>
<li><b>Fibres and circuits in 3D</b>: fibre components, circuit parts and chips stand on the table in the 3D view, each a box with its symbol on its top, ferrules and pins at its ports, and their fibres, wires and waveguides laid along their routes, rising to each port (a fibre glows the colour of its light). No tab stays in 2D now. The parts’ names in 3D are off to start with (View › Names in 3D).</li>
<li><b>More room on the bench</b>: the parts rail is a bar across the top, every palette’s groups along it as small icons (free space, fibre, circuits and RF at once), its switcher now changing the mode: Parts or Draw (2D); the bench’s tabs sit at the bottom left and the 2D / 3D switch at the bottom right. The Bench panel lists each bench’s parts on a tab of its own. The 3D view’s Fly, mouse and picture buttons are icons in the bar beside Fit, Measure and Search, and its names are under View. Free space’s mirrors and lenses are two groups, and <b>+ Add</b> keeps the parts added lately in a <b>Recent</b> tab of their own.</li>
<li><b>A tidier Position section</b>: a part’s place is two rows of three, X, Y, Z and Angle, Tip, Roll, each with its name over it and room for the whole number; its angle is called Angle on every part, a line under it saying what it means for that one.</li>
<li><b>The lens panel</b>: the lens drawn to scale at its top (its faces’ radii, thickness and diameter on it, each glass tinted, a coated face in colour; click a face for its radius), and a warning when its faces cross before the rim; its shape and glass, diameter and thickness two to a row; its faces as a small table, a row each with its radius and coating and a ▸ for the rest (clear radius, Fresnel rings, the coating’s numbers, aspheric terms), and a row for each glass between faces; and its <b>focal length</b> typed to set, its faces scaled together so it keeps its form (an asphere’s terms and a diffractive lens’s phase with them). An axicon has its cone angle up top.</li>
<li><b>Clearer part panels</b>: each measuring part says what it reads in one line under its name (a detector’s mW, a screen’s spot, a lens’s focal length, a fibre’s coupling); a lens has its thickness and glass with its diameter and each face its radius and coating, the rest in a fold; a mirror’s conic, aspheric terms, hole, off-axis offset and GDD fold away until set; a source’s settings come as Light, Rays, Gaussian beam, Polarisation and coherence, and Pulse; a photodetector in tabs; a source’s and a lamp’s settings two to a row (wavelength beside power, width beside divergence, a lamp’s shape beside its size), their more wavelengths typed or picked from a set, in one row; a source’s polarisation drawn as seen along its beam; a new source’s rays in <b>hexapolar rings</b> across its beam (Rays across the beam; a saved bench keeps its own); sizes called Diameter (or Width, for a mirror, screen or grating) on every part, each panel in one order (what kind, what it does, its size, its material); and no empty sections.</li>
<li><b>Fresnel lenses</b>: give a lens’s curved face <b>Fresnel rings</b> (mm) and it is cut into rings of that pitch, each with the face’s slope, as a moulded Fresnel lens is: it focuses as the solid lens does, a fraction as thick, a little light lost at the risers. And: a <b>Lamp</b> (Add part › Lamp: a sphere or a cylinder of its size, standing, lying or tilted, shining every way from its surface, in 3D, its body taking light that comes back to it; and a <b>Circular lamp</b>, a point shining round the bench plane only, quick for 2D benches); an <b>angular size</b> (the sun’s half a degree, so its image is a disc); mirrors that <b>absorb</b> (Passes through: what is neither reflected nor passed is lost); a group that <b>spins</b> about one of its parts (Turn the group, its Spin a sweep to play); <b>Ray width</b> and <b>Rays glow</b> under Bench › Light; and screens’ <b>beam direction</b> and <b>arrival angle</b>, for the optimiser and the exercises.</li>
<li><b>Exercises</b>: <b>Help › Exercises</b> has eleven short exercises on ready-made benches, from aiming a mirror to fixing a fibre’s polarisation. Each says what to reach and reads it as you go, has two hints, and holds every part but the ones it is about until you leave it. Solved ones are ticked, and kept with a free account. Under them, <b>Challenges</b>: the puzzles from our Instagram reels, newest first, starting with “Can you hit the pinhole?”; the same checks and hints, kept apart from the course.</li>
<li><b>For recording</b>: <b>Rays as bright as their power</b> (Bench › Light) draws every ray against the strongest on the bench, so light fades as a filter or splitter takes it, and <b>Fading trails</b> leaves where the rays were as a part moves or a sweep plays. Open the page with <code>?kiosk</code> (or <code>JEKray.kiosk(true)</code>) for the bench alone, and <b>View › Names a fixed size on screen</b> keeps names one size as you zoom. Scripts gain <code>J.set(name, { … })</code>, <code>J.setFibre</code>, <code>J.setView</code>, <code>J.renderPNG</code>, labelled <code>J.rays()</code>, <code>J.distance</code>, and bench coordinates from <code>J.hitsOn</code>.</li>
<li><b>More prisms</b>: the pentaprism (90° whatever its tilt), the Amici roof prism, the Pellin–Broca prism and a polygon of your own corners, with any faces silvered. Mirrors can have a <b>hole through them</b>, a source’s line of rays can carry <b>power as across a round beam</b> (so an iris passes what it would), and a fibre wound round a radius has its <b>bend loss</b> (Marcuse’s formula, single-mode fibre). A fibre’s route now moves with the parts at its ends.</li>
<li><b>Fixed</b>: a fibre path set from a script without its handles no longer stops the bench drawing; the empty bench’s tip steps aside for the parts picker; names on the bench keep a gap between them; a short mirror’s hatching no longer fills it.</li>
<li><b>Try JEKrayPro on a free account</b>: each month a free account gets a few uses of the design work, to try it: 5 optimiser runs in the Optical and RF designers, 3 tolerance runs, 10 script runs, 3 design reports, 3 drawing saves, 3 design exports and 5 Excel, NumPy or MATLAB data exports. The Pro badge says how many are left (“4 free”). Once the month’s optimiser runs are used, the optimiser still runs as a <b>preview</b>: see the better design, then keep it with JEKrayPro or put the design back. A free account also keeps <b>3 share links</b> at once. And a <b>founding member price</b>: subscribe during the open beta and keep your price for as long as you stay subscribed.</li>
<li><b>Signing in, where it helps</b>: signed out, asking for something that needs an account (My benches, the experimental features) or JEKrayPro (the optimiser, scripts, the cloud, My parts) now says what it needs, with one-click ways in, rather than just opening the account menu; and the end of a tour and the first-visit welcome note offer a free account too.</li>
<li><b>From Instagram</b>: following a link from one of our Instagram posts shows the benches from our latest reels, each a click away (close the note and it stays closed until a new reel is added). And once you have changed a bench, signed out, a note offers a free account, once a visit, for what it gives: exporting the bench’s images and data, making part packs and the experimental features. Your bench stays as it is while you sign in.</li>
<li><b>Square links</b>, as in a schematic: tick <b>View › Lay new links square</b> and a new fibre, wire or waveguide is laid click by click, from its port through a corner at each click to the port it ends on, running only across and up the bench. Links already laid keep their way; a link’s panel has <b>Route</b> (Curved or Square) to change just that one.</li>
<li><b>Export figure</b>: <b>File › Export figure…</b> makes the bench a figure for where it is going. <b>Journal</b>: white, no holes, line art, the light in its colour or black, the names in Helvetica at a size in points, 85 mm (one column) or 174 mm (two) wide, no line under 0.5 pt, a scale bar; PDF, SVG or a 600 dpi PNG. <b>Technical drawing</b>: an A4 or A3 sheet to a standard scale, the parts’ centres dimensioned, numbered callouts, a parts list and a title block. <b>Presentation</b>: the bench as it looks on a 16:9 or 4:3 slide. A preview shows each before it comes down.</li>
<li><b>Find a part by what it does</b>: Add part’s search and Ctrl+K know what each part is for, so “focus” finds the lenses, “measure power” the photodetectors and “frequency doubling” the nonlinear crystal; parts named for what was typed come first.</li>
<li><b>Lines and arrows</b>: the Draw palette gains <b>Line</b> (L) and <b>Arrow</b> (W), straight at a drag (Ctrl for steps of 15°), and any open path can end in an arrowhead, a dot or a bar; right-click on empty bench for <b>Add a note here</b> and <b>Add an arrow here</b>. The bench’s name sits in the middle of the page when the bar has room.</li>
<li><b>Add part moves to the parts rail</b>, as its topmost button: the picker opens beside it, every part with a search (A still opens it, and View › Add a part). The bar keeps the menus, the bench’s name, Share and Save.</li>
<li><b>One palette switcher</b>: the parts rail’s five coloured buttons become one switcher at its top, showing the palette in use with its icon; it opens a list of the palettes, each with a line of what it holds. Electronics is now called <b>Circuits</b>.</li>
<li><b>Smaller things</b>: the menus answer the keyboard (Down opens one and walks it, Left and Right move between them); <b>Ctrl+K</b> finds parts and examples as well as commands; Undo and Redo say what they would do (“Undo move Laser”); <b>File › Open recent</b> lists the files, examples and cloud benches opened lately; with several parts selected, <b>Set them all</b> sets a height, a facing, a diameter or a wavelength on every one; a part dragged near another lines up with it, or with a beam, a faint guide showing it (Shift drags freely); opening something over unsaved changes says where they were kept, and leaving the page with them asks first; in 3D, the names, the hint and the colour key follow the theme.</li>
<li><b>Parts in 3D look as they do in a lab</b> in the Light theme: brighter light from a warm sky, black-anodised housings (lasers, photodiodes, mounts) a mid grey that shades, and mirrors and other metal a satin silver rather than dark discs.</li>
<li><b>The Bench panel pulls out from the side</b>: a small arrow tab half way up the bench’s right edge brings out the bench’s settings (light, snapping, notes and the parts list), and, with any panel out, puts it away again; it rides on the panel’s edge, its arrow turned. It takes the place of the gear in the corner. On a phone it is a handle at the bottom that pulls the sheet up.</li>
<li><b>A light theme, and it is the default</b>: the bench is warm paper, with the rail, the minimap and the 3D view to match, and the light drawn in clear, vivid colours that never muddy to black where they cross; white light is drawn grey until a prism or a grating parts its colours, as a book draws it. The dark breadboard is the <b>Dark</b> theme. <b>View › Theme</b> picks Light, Dark or as the computer is set; the choice is yours, kept in this browser, so a bench opens in your theme whoever made it (a colour a bench was saved with is no longer used). Exported pictures come out in your theme.</li>
<li><b>A full dark mode</b>: in the <b>Dark</b> theme the whole page is dark, not just the bench: the bar and its menus, the panels, the plots, the dialogs, and the Optical, RF and coating designers, with the browser’s own fields and scrollbars to match.</li>
<li><b>A tidier bar</b>: a menu bar, <b>File, Edit, View, Tools, Sweeps and Help</b>, as a desktop program has, with icons for undo, redo, fit, measure and search beside it, and the bench’s name in the middle. <b>Edit</b> holds cut, copy, paste, duplicate, delete, select all, rotate and grouping; <b>Tools</b> the Optical, RF and coating designers, Scripts and the bench’s settings. <b>Ctrl+K</b> (or the magnifier) searches every command in the menus by its words: type “export” or “3D” and press Enter.</li>
<li><b>Export data</b>: <b>File › Export data…</b> writes the numbers behind the bench as files for a spreadsheet, Python or MATLAB: its <b>readouts</b> (every screen, detector, spectrometer and antenna, one table), its <b>plots</b>’ curves, each screen’s <b>ray hits</b> and <b>field map</b>, its <b>Gaussian beams</b> (q, size, waist and divergence along the way), its <b>sweeps</b> and studies, and <b>the bench</b> itself, every part with its settings. Each file says what it holds: the bench, the version, the date, every column’s unit and the settings of the parts the numbers come from. CSV (a zip, with a README) and JSON need a free account, one kind at a time; <b>Excel, NumPy and MATLAB</b> files, several kinds at once and <b>Export everything</b> are JEKrayPro’s. In Scripts, <code>save(name, data, format)</code> keeps what a script makes as a file in any of the five formats, downloaded when the run ends (nothing when it is stopped), and a result’s <b>Save as</b> offers them all.</li>
<li><b>Scripts run in the background, with Stop</b> (JEKrayPro): Tools › Scripts… runs a script, JavaScript or Python, beside the page on a copy of the bench, so a long loop no longer holds the page. While it runs, Run becomes <b>Stop</b>, with the time it has run, and its <code>log()</code> and <code>print()</code> lines come as they are written; Stop ends it at once and applies nothing. When it ends, what it changed is applied as one step, which one Undo puts back. <code>J.sweepPlay</code>, which plays a sweep on the bench in view, needs the page: such a script can be run there instead (no Stop).</li>
<li><b>Right-drag pans the bench</b>, as middle-drag and Space-drag do; a right-click that does not drag still opens the menu.</li>
<li><b>Signed part packs</b>: a pack made in JEKray is signed with your account (a free one is enough), so whoever installs it sees <b>✓ Signed by the JEKray account ‘</b>your name<b>’</b>, and that it has not been changed since (the name is your account’s own, so it is shown plainly, not as checked). A pack edited by hand afterwards reads <b>Unverified: changed after it was signed</b>: sign it again with File › Part packs and modules… › <b>Sign a pack file…</b>, which also signs a module you wrote. A pack’s id is its maker’s once signed: a pack with that id installs only when its maker signed it, which stops someone else’s pack posing as or replacing yours (ids starting jek., jekray. and jeksys. are JEKray’s own). A <b>module installs only when signed and unchanged</b>, from a file, a link or a bench; one installed before keeps working, labelled Unverified. JEK Systems can revoke a harmful pack (installed packs are checked once a day: a revoked module is turned off), and <b>Report this pack</b> tells us of one. Teams on JEKrayPro can sign as their organisation, shown as <b>✓ Verified: </b><i>organisation</i><b> (</b><i>domain</i><b>)</b>, once they have verified their web domain themselves: a DNS record, set up from the team’s settings under <b>Signing packs as the team</b>.</li>
<li><b>Making a part pack</b> needs a free account, as exports do; installing a pack needs none.</li>
<li><b>Exports need a free account</b>: File › Export layout (PNG, SVG, PDF), the 3D view’s PNG, every plot’s PNG and CSV, a screen’s Export data (CSV), File › Export an element (.zmx) and an assembly’s CAD files (.step, .stl) ask you to sign in first; a free account is enough. Saving the bench as a .jekray file needs no account, as before. And <b>badges</b> say what needs what: <b>Free account</b> and <b>Pro</b>, on the buttons and menu items concerned, each gone once you have it.</li>
<li><b>A rolled cylindrical lens keeps its power at every roll</b>: rolled, it lost some or all of its power at many angles (a curved-in-plane cylinder’s face was missed by rays off its rolled axis; a curved-out-of-plane one was met as flat). And on a <b>phosphor screen</b>, a line now glows as a thin line whichever way it lies (a horizontal one blurred into a wide patch), and a rolled screen’s glow in 3D stays where the light lands.</li>
<li><b>Python in Scripts</b> (JEKrayPro): File › Scripts… runs Python as well as JavaScript, chosen for each script beside its name. It is given the same <code>J</code>, its answers as dicts and lists, and <code>log()</code> (and <code>print()</code>); what it sets <code>result</code> to, or its last line’s value, is shown, rows as a table with Save as CSV. <code>import numpy</code> works, and NumPy arrays are taken as lists. An error shows Python’s traceback for the script’s own lines. Python (Pyodide) runs in this browser, fetched from this site the first time a Python script runs (13.5 MB, and NumPy 3.0 MB more, once); nothing leaves it. The examples come in Python too.</li>
<li><b>STEP files</b> come in as STL objects: Open ▾ → Import an object (.stl, .step), or drop a .step or .stp file on the bench. OpenCascade reads it (fetched the first time, 7.6 MB, and run in the background), in the file’s own units; a file of several parts asks whether to bring them in as separate parts, grouped and in place, or as one object.</li>
<li>On a phone, <b>the tour no longer pushes the tool sideways</b>: its note was wider than the screen beside the parts rail, which shifted the bench and clipped the first tab; it now fits between the rail and the edge.</li>
<li><b>What a free account gives</b>, said wherever sign-in is offered: the experimental features, and joining a team you are invited to; with a university email, JEKrayPro where your university has a licence, or else the academic price. Signing in the first time, with Google, Microsoft or an emailed code, makes the account. A bench restored from this browser on a later visit, signed out, says it is kept here alone and offers a file or an account (once a week at most, as the other notes); a shared bench’s bar has <b>Save a copy</b>, to the cloud with JEKrayPro, or as a file; and the tour’s last step has <b>Save this bench</b>.</li>
<li>The welcome note and the tour have a <b>× to close them</b> in their corner, and a shared bench or example opened into a page already open closes the welcome note (on a phone it could stay over the bench).</li>
<li><b>Phosphor screen</b>, beside the screen in the picker: its face glows where the light lands and fades after it, to 1/e in its decay time, so a beam swept across it by a sweep or a drag leaves a trail. Its decay time and glow colour are in its panel. The glow keeps up with the rays at any speed, or follows the diffracted field when the bench shows it, and in 3D it is always on the screen’s face.</li>
<li><b>Experimental features for every account</b>: the switch under Help › Experimental features… now needs only a signed-in account, a free one or JEKrayPro, where before it needed a plan.</li>
<li>On a phone, the welcome note can <b>email you a link for your computer</b>, where JEKray has room for its designers and plots; the address is used for that one email and not kept. Signed out, <b>Share</b> says what a short link needs and offers sign-in or a .jekray file instead, and a file Save offers sign-in for cloud saving (once a week at most).</li>
<li>In 3D, <b>the diffracted field of interfering beams runs to its end</b>: a beam’s last stretch, up to where it meets a screen, could be left without its fringes when its length happened to round up by a millionth of a millimetre, so an interferometer’s pattern stopped short of its screen and only the beam’s own glow went on.</li>
<li><b>Collimator</b>, in the fibre palette (Ends and links) and beside the fibre tip in free space: a fibre tip with its lens, so a fibre network’s light leaves as a collimated beam (0.6 mm in radius at 1550 nm for the usual f = 11 mm) with no lens to place and focus, and a beam coming back couples in by that beam’s mode. Any fibre tip takes a <b>Collimating lens f</b>; 0 keeps it bare.</li>
<li>The <b>fibre Bragg grating</b> is a real grating now, by coupled-mode theory: give its length, Bragg wavelength and index modulation δn, and it reflects tanh²(κL) at its peak (κ = π v δn / λ), with its side lobes and the zeros between them, and what it reflects and passes carries its phase, so its delay and dispersion; a modulator’s sidebands meet it at their own frequencies. Its panel shows κL, the peak reflectance, the band between the first zeros, the width at half the peak, the period and the delay. <b>Apodisation</b> (Gaussian or raised cosine) takes the side lobes down and a <b>chirp</b> spreads the band and its delay. A bench saved before, with the grating as a Gaussian band of a set width and peak, opens with that band (Model: Simple band) and reads as it did.</li>
<li>A source’s <b>Edge softness</b>: without a Gaussian beam, the diffracted field of its ray fan is a uniform top-hat, and its edge now rises over a set distance (10% to 90%). <b>Automatic</b>, the default, is just enough for the field grid: before, the hard edge rang on the grid, showing rings across a wide beam (about 1%) that were not in the light. Set 0 for a hard edge, or more for a lamp behind a soft aperture. A changed edge also redraws the field, which it had not.</li>
<li><b>Fringe visibility</b> on a screen, from its rays and from the diffracted field, is now the textbook one: twice the cross terms between the paths of one laser over the sum of their powers, 2√(I₁I₂)/(I₁ + I₂) for two beams, where they overlap. Before, it was read from the brightest and dimmest points, so two separate lasers overlapping (brighter where one lies on another) read as fringes, a single beam’s own profile read as a third, and fringes finer than the map read low or at random as the pixels fell on them. The diffracted map is also drawn finer where fringes are fine, up to 1024 points across.</li>
<li><b>Spectrometer</b>, in Sources and detectors: a slit or fibre entrance and a detector array, showing the light through it as counts against wavelength, with the peak, its width, the resolution, the light that gets in, saturation and the signal-to-noise. <b>Kind</b> picks a typical instrument (compact UV to near-infrared, high-resolution visible, fibre-coupled visible, near-infrared or short-wave infrared) and any setting can then be changed. A narrower slit sharpens the lines and lets less light in, as on the real thing. The new example <b>Czerny–Turner spectrometer</b> builds one from a slit, two concave mirrors and a grating, beside the part reading the same lamp.</li>
<li><b>On a phone or tablet</b>: the bench fills the screen, and a part’s settings open in a sheet over its lower half (↑ makes it taller, × or a tap on the empty bench closes it), the part moved clear of the sheet if it would be under it. A phone on its side has the one-row bar too. The welcome note, the parts picker and the menus say tap rather than click, and that JEKray is best used on a desktop or laptop, where the designers, plots and shortcuts have the room they need.</li>
<li>A lens surface’s <b>hole radius</b> is set in the Optical designer only; the bench panel shows it when there is one. A hole as wide as the surface or wider (which left the face drawn but not there for the light) is no hole. And a lens with a plain hole through a face, nothing stacked in it, no longer stops the bench from tracing.</li>
<li>In the Optical designer, <b>Insert a surface</b> and <b>Remove</b> now work on a lens with stacked faces or mirror coats: the new surface goes on the part itself, after the one selected the way the light goes on from it (back into the glass off a mirror), and the part’s later surfaces keep their variables and solves. Before, the change was lost. The <b>Insert a surface</b> and <b>Insert an element</b> menus also stay open when clicked: the pointer had opened them and the click shut them again.</li>
<li><b>Layers on a face</b>: stacked surfaces of the same clear radius and hole are now layers, met one after the other in the order the light comes to them, on the bench, in the diffracted field and in the Optical designer. Before, only the first was there and the rest were ignored, coatings and all: a partly reflecting coating on a second layer now reflects, a bare face over a mirror coat reflects its share of light from behind, and a layer with the same glass either side is on the light’s path and changes nothing.</li>
<li><b>Anonymous usage counts</b>: JEKray now counts which of its features are used (parts added by type, designers, analyses and examples opened, exports by format) and its own errors, so we can see what to improve. The counts carry nothing that says who you are, are not linked to your account and never include your benches, their names or anything you type. None are sent from an embedded bench or when your browser asks sites not to track it, and you can turn them off in the account menu (<b>Share anonymous usage counts</b>) or on the Your account page. See the Privacy Policy.</li>
<li><b>Clear radii and holes for the optimiser</b>: a lens surface’s clear radius and hole radius each have a <b>V</b> in the Optical designer, and the merit a new term, <b>Light reaching the image</b>: the share of the entrance pupil whose rays get through every clear radius and hole, worked out so it changes smoothly. With both, the optimiser sizes a telescope’s spot, the window in its primary and its mirrors together (a stacked surface varied, its stack follows).</li>
<li><b>Stacked surfaces in the Optical designer as on the bench</b>: each stacked surface is analysed only over the ring where it is the surface met, so a window stacked in a primary’s hole is clipped at the hole (a telescope whose exit cone is wider than its window now shows the light it loses, as the bench always did). The part keeps its own clear radius and hole. Where two stacked surfaces overlap, the one with the smaller clear radius is the surface there (a spot reaches its own rim whatever the hole under it; before, a ring whose hole was smaller than the spot took over part of it), the same in the bench’s rays, the drawings, the field and the designer. The designer’s layout draws rays the light really takes: where the usual five heights across the pupil are stopped (a telescope’s secondary in the middle), five spread over the heights that get through.</li>
<li><b>The diffracted field through a solid telescope</b>: a face built of stacked surfaces or with a hole is now taken ring by ring, the beam split into a branch for each ring, its field cut to the ring and passed through that ring’s own surface. Before, the field followed the beam’s centre alone, which a telescope’s secondary sends straight back, so in 2D and 3D nothing came out. The bench’s field also keeps a surface’s whole light on its grid when what gets through is much wider than the beam it is fitted to (it had cut a telescope’s converging ring in half at the secondary), the 2D view slices beams that run together at each one’s own steps (a focus close behind a part was missed), and an assembly with mirrors in it gives its focal lengths along the light’s own path on its panel and in the command line.</li>
<li><b>Stop stops</b>: the <b>Stop</b> button of the optimiser, tolerancing and Monte Carlo in the Optical and RF designers now acts as it is pressed, and the tables update a few times a second while a run goes on. <b>Image plane held still</b>: a solve for the image distance (<b>…</b> beside it) keeps the image plane a set distance from the first surface, so the optimiser and typed gaps move the lenses and not the image. <b>Image simulation</b> works for telescopes whose secondary blocks the centre of the beam, and for a design with only a field on the axis (a patch about the axis), and a design with one wavelength keeps the picture’s colours (it had shown the red channel in grey).</li>
<li><b>Short share links</b> (JEKrayPro): <b>Share link</b> makes a short link, <i>jeksys.net/s/</i> and ten letters, that opens the bench as it is now for anyone, with no account needed, and an embed code made from it. Each link is a snapshot of the bench as it was; the same bench gives the same link again. <b>My links</b>, in My benches, lists your links with how often each has been opened, to open, copy or delete (a deleted link stops opening at once), as does the Share dialog. The <b>Try me</b> QR code is the short link too, so any bench fits in it. Links made before, with the bench in them, still open.</li>
<li><b>The designers’ design work is now part of JEKrayPro</b>: in the Optical and RF designers, the optimiser (with its global search and glass substitution), tolerancing, design reports, lens drawings and exporting a design as a lens file need a plan (your own JEKrayPro, an Academic or team plan, or a university licence), and their buttons are marked <b>Pro</b> until you sign in with one. Opening the designers, building and editing a design and every analysis stay open to everyone, as do an RF lens’s way to a quote and the whole coating designer. Your designs always open. The JEKray Licence (1.1) and JEKrayPro Terms (1.5) say so.</li>
<li><b>Surfaces with holes, stacked surfaces and mirror coatings</b>: each lens surface now has a <b>clear radius</b>, a <b>hole radius</b> (inside it the surface is not there) and a coating that can be a <b>mirror</b> (ideal, aluminium, silver or gold, with the metal’s reflectance) or a dielectric high reflector. A surface given a thickness of <b>0</b> is <b>stacked</b> on the one before: the two share a vertex and make one face, each where it reaches, so a flat with a hole and a mirror-coated spot stacked in it is a solid telescope’s front, and a lens whose back is mirror coated is a Mangin mirror. The <b>Optical designer</b> works out the path the light takes through such a lens and shows two tables: the <b>Surfaces</b>, each once in the part’s own order with its coating, clear radius and hole to type, and <b>the light’s path</b>, each meeting in order with what is clear and blocked there; <b>Stack a surface</b> puts a surface in the centre of the one selected. Lens drawings show a stacked face as one, with its holes and coatings. The <i>Mirrored</i> setting a face had is gone: a bench saved with it opens as the surfaces it stood for, stacked. A thickness between parts may be negative.</li>
<li><b>Fibre tips</b> have a source’s two ticks for the light they send out: <b>Trace the ray fan</b> and <b>Propagate a Gaussian beam</b>, each with its settings under it, so a tip can show rays alone or a beam alone.</li>
<li><b>Scripts on the bench</b> (JEKrayPro): <b>File › Scripts…</b> opens an editor where JavaScript runs against the bench with the documented calls: read a screen or a detector, move a part and read again, sweep a parameter to a table saved as CSV, or check a figure. Scripts are kept in this browser by name, or as .js files; Undo puts the bench back after a run.</li>
<li><b>A JEKray account of your own</b>: sign in with an email address and a password, beside Google and Microsoft, for anyone whose university does not let them sign in with Microsoft (the “Need admin approval” page) or who has neither account. New here, or forgotten the password? Ask for a 6-digit code by email, type it, and you are in, choosing a password as you go if you like; set, change or remove it on your account page. Passwords are kept only as salted hashes, and ten wrong ones lock the address for a quarter of an hour. Someone already signed in links an address from the account menu, and a university address counts for its licence and the academic price as before.</li>
<li><b>Names</b>: the lens design workspace is the <b>Optical designer</b> (it designs mirrors, windows and stops as well as lenses), a part is opened in it with <b>Design as an assembly…</b> and an RF part with <b>Design as an RF assembly…</b>, and the .zmx menu items read <b>Import an element</b> and <b>Export an element</b>. <b>Element data</b>: <b>Insert a surface</b> offers the kind of surface (flat, spherical, conic, freeform, diffractive, graded glass), <b>Duplicate surface type</b> repeats the selected one’s kind, and <b>Insert an element</b> offers the bench’s asphere, diffractive lens, GRIN rod lens and cylindrical lens as well as a singlet. <b>Experimental features</b> are part of JEKrayPro.</li>
<li><b>Fibre tips</b> have a source’s field settings (its model and grid points) for the beam they send out. <b>Fly</b> keeps you upright: the mouse looks round about the room’s up and tips the view to just short of straight up or down, never rolled, and Space and Ctrl move straight up and down. A screen’s <b>Diffraction</b> map is drawn on the screen’s own face, at its true size and place (zoom in for the spot’s detail). In 3D an RF metal mirror is the colour of its metal, and a made-to-order lens’s flange shows its bolt holes.</li>
<li><b>Scripting and headless use</b>: the engine runs in Node without a browser (<code>headless.mjs</code>), and a command line (<code>cli.mjs</code>) traces a bench file and prints its readouts, the RF designer’s figures, or a parameter sweep as CSV, with the lens designer’s analyses (focal lengths, spots, wavefronts, MTF, field curves, the merit function, lens files) and the RF designer’s figures, so a design can be checked in a repository and a parameter study can be a loop; the page’s <code>window.JEKray</code> calls that are kept stable are now listed in the docs.</li>
<li><b>Steadier flying, a plainer chopper</b>: Q and E no longer roll the view in Fly, a rolling picture having made people queasy; the optical chopper’s blades are filled where they block the beam, open where its slots let light by (their share its duty): in 3D they had been drawn hollow.</li>
<li><b>Brightness follows power</b>: a ray is drawn as bright as the power it carries to the 0.4, and a Gaussian beam’s envelope fades with its share of the source’s power, so the two arms of a polarising split are seen trading power as a waveplate turns (before, a beam kept nearly its full brightness down to a tenth of the power and then went out within a few degrees). A 4% ghost still shows at about a third of the brightness; a beam 40 dB down is a trace.</li>
<li><b>An RF design report</b>: <b>Report (PDF)</b> in the RF designer writes the design as one PDF to hand on, as the optical designer’s does: its conditions and figures, the layout and where the power goes, Element data with the merit and configurations, its analyses, tolerances and sensitivity, what can be made, and each lens’s drawing.</li>
<li><b>Four more RF analyses</b>: a <b>phase map</b> of the wavefront error over the beam; the <b>cross-polar</b> field the system makes, followed ray by ray from a balanced horn through each face’s Fresnel amplitudes and each mirror’s reflection (a lens’s from its faces, an offset reflector’s from its geometry); the <b>beam to the goal</b>, its radius along the way and where its waist falls; and the design over <b>temperature</b>, each lens grown by its plastic’s expansion and the air by the housing’s, with the feed refocused or not.</li>
<li><b>Configurations in the RF designer</b>: the system in several states, as the optical designer has them: a second band, a switched feed, another goal, each configuration with its own conditions and its own values of the Element data you choose to differ, everything else shared. The merit adds them up by weight, Optimise finds each configuration’s own values and the shared ones together, and the one shown is the bench’s.</li>
<li><b>Mirrors in the RF designer</b>: a curved mirror is a member like a lens: its radius and conic are edited in Element data and can be variables for Optimise. An <b>offset reflector</b> is traced as the section it is (the parent’s face with its vertex off the axis, the beam meeting it at the part’s centre), with its first-order power about the beam’s centre, so a paraboloid fed from its focus comes out flat and its offset can be varied too; typed on a whole curved mirror, an offset makes it a section where it stands.</li>
<li><b>A merit function for the RF designer</b>: a <b>Merit</b> tab, as the optical designer has, where what Optimise works toward is a table of terms, each a figure of the system (efficiency, gain or coupling, edge taper, phase error, spillover, reflections, sidelobe, beamwidth, the beam steered, scan loss, a waist, a thickness, a distance) at one frequency or across the band, with a target, a sense and a weight, its value now and its share of the merit; the boundaries live there too. With no terms it is the efficiency across the band, as before.</li>
<li><b>The RF designer scans</b>: the feed horn can stand <b>off the axis</b>, aimed at the first lens, and the beam leaves steered the other way: the figures give its direction, the beam deviation factor and the scan loss against the feed on the axis, the layout shows the beam walking across the lenses, and <b>Analyses › Scan</b> takes the feed round in steps. The beam’s centre is followed through the system beside the Gaussian beam, so spillover and aperture efficiency are those of a beam off centre, and the phase error is that of the rays from where the feed stands. <b>Tolerance</b> takes errors across the axis too (a lens decentred or tilted, the feed moved across), says how far each turns the beam, and can refocus the feed for each build as a compensator.</li>
<li>The RF designer has an <b>Element data</b> tab, as the optical designer has its element data: every surface in one table, from the feed horn to the goal, each radius, conic, thickness and material typed there, and the <b>V</b> beside a value marking it as a variable for <b>Optimise</b>, which now lists what it will vary.</li>
<li>The File menu’s two lens-file imports are one: <b>Import a lens (.zmx)…</b>, whose dialog has a tick to open the file in the lens design workspace as an assembly to design.</li>
<li>Menu items that need an account or JEKrayPro (<b>My benches</b>, <b>Save to cloud</b>, <b>Fork this bench</b>, <b>Save to My parts</b>, the designers’ <b>Keep as a part</b>) are now always there, greyed when they are not possible with a word on why (sign in, or subscribe); choosing one opens the way to make it so.</li>
<li>A lens’s panel now gives its focal lengths at the wavelengths whose light reaches it, rather than at every source’s on the bench; a lens nothing reaches says so, and gives them at the bench’s wavelengths.</li>
<li><b>Open a workspace</b>, on the File menu, gathers the designers: lens design (new, or of the selection), RF design (new, or of the selected RF parts) and coating design. On <b>My benches</b>, <b>Open a workspace</b> makes a new cloud bench in the folder shown and opens it straight into the designer chosen. Each designer’s header has <b>Keep as a part…</b>, which saves the whole design (its parts, with their conditions and design) by name in <b>My parts</b> or, with a team, in that team’s <b>Team parts</b> on My benches, from where it is added to any bench; Save to My parts on the right-click menu offers the same choice.</li>
<li><b>A coating workspace</b>: design a thin-film coating (an anti-reflection stack, a high reflector, a beam splitter, a dichroic edge or an RF matching layer) on its substrate, judged over a band of wavelengths and a range of angles, its reflectance plotted across the band and against the angle, s and p, and its thicknesses optimised; it is traced with the one thin-film model the bench and both designers use. Open it from any face’s <b>Coating</b> setting (<b>Design a coating…</b>), from the lens designer’s Polarisation face table, from <b>Design…</b> beside the RF designer’s matching layers, or on its own from <b>File › Open a workspace</b>; <b>Use this coating</b> writes the stack to the face it came from, and <b>Keep as a coating…</b> saves it by name for every face’s Coating list.</li>
<li><b>Offset reflectors and radomes</b> in the RF palette: a section of a paraboloid cut off its axis, whose panel gives its focal length, the turn it gives the beam and where its focus is, so the horn can be put there; and a radome sheet, whose panel gives what it passes square on and at the beam’s angle and the half-wave thicknesses that pass everything but its loss. A curved RF mirror on its axis now gives its figures as an antenna, as a lens does, and the RF designer counts a metal mirror’s ohmic loss.</li>
<li><b>A graded-index disc and a zoned lens, traced as they are made.</b> The bench now traces a graded-index RF disc as a slab of graded plastic between two flat faces (the same slab the RF designer and the lens engine take, so the three agree on where it focuses), with each part’s loss at its own density and each face’s matching layer at the radius met; and a zoned lens as it is cut, its curved face stepped back where whole layers come out, each step a sheer wall that shadows the rays and the diffracted field behind it. The 2D outline shows the steps, and the RF designer traces the same cut face: its walls’ shadow and its zones’ small defocus now count in its efficiency.</li>
<li>The bench’s <b>Tolerance the bench</b> study is now seeded by the number of builds asked for, so running it again gives the same spread; the lens designer’s and the RF designer’s Monte Carlo draw from the same seeded source. Under the surface, one copy each of the surface sag, the Bessel functions, the small linear solvers and the complex arithmetic now serves the bench, both designers and the drawings, and the RF designer’s gain is checked against the bench’s closed form for a lens antenna.</li>
<li><b>One set of numbers for every face</b>: the bench’s rays, its diffracted field and focus, the lens designer’s polarisation trace and the RF designer’s reflections now take a face’s s and p amplitudes from one place, so they agree exactly. Light through a <b>coated face</b> now keeps the coating’s own phase, so a beamsplitter or AR stack met at a slant retards p against s on the way through, as a real one does; a coated face now reflects s and p with the same sign square on (p was turned over before); the lens designer’s mirrors reflect their own reflectance; and the RF designer counts any coating stack on a lens, not only a single matching layer.</li>
<li>A tidier interface: <b>three kinds of button</b> (one solid button for the main action, outlined ones for the others, and plain words for menus and toggles), <b>Save</b> marked with a dot when the bench has changed since it was opened or saved, and the designers’ tabs drawn as tabs. On a <b>phone</b> the top bar is one row: the bench’s name, <b>+</b>, <b>Save</b> and <b>⋯</b>, a menu holding the rest. The <b>RF designer</b> lists its system down the left as the beam meets it (the frequency, the feed horn, each lens, the goal) and edits the one chosen beside the beam; <b>Add a lens</b> puts another after the last and designs it, and a lens can be taken out again.</li>
